title: The Price of Buttermilk
summary: A dishonest milkman waters down his milk to double his profits. A clever monkey ensures poetic justice by dividing the ill-gotten gains.
full_text:
In a village along the road to Delhi lived an unscrupulous milkman named Ganga Ram. Every morning, before filling his brass canisters to sell buttermilk to travelers and pilgrims, Ganga Ram stopped at the canal and added an equal amount of dirty river water to the churned buttermilk, doubling his volume and tripling his profit.

When customers complained that the buttermilk tasted watery, Ganga Ram swore on his ancestors: 'I swear by the holy river that this buttermilk is as pure as morning dew!'

Over five years of deceit, Ganga Ram accumulated a heavy leather bag filled with five hundred silver rupees. Smug and wealthy, he decided to travel to the grand festival in Agra to buy gold jewelry for his wife.

On his journey, the afternoon sun beat down with scorching fury. Tired and sweating, Ganga Ram stopped under a sprawling banyan tree beside a deep, clear river. He placed his precious moneybag on a flat rock, took off his clothes, and jumped into the cool water to bathe.

High up in the banyan branches sat a troop of mischievous monkeys. The alpha monkey, seeing the shiny leather bag, scrambled down the trunk, snatched the bag, and leaped to the topmost branch!

Ganga Ram splashed out of the water, screaming in terror: 'Drop that bag, you cursed ape! That is my life's fortune!'

He hurled stones and fruit at the monkey, but the animal only chattered angrily. The monkey untied the leather drawstring, reached inside, and pulled out a handful of silver coins.

Looking down at the frantic milkman, the monkey dropped one silver coin onto the dry grass where Ganga Ram stood. Then, swinging to the outer branch, the monkey dropped the next silver coin into the deep river water! *Plop!*

The monkey continued methodically: one coin dropped to the earth, one coin thrown into the river. One for the land, one for the water.

Ganga Ram wept and tore his hair as two hundred and fifty silver coins sank forever to the muddy river bottom, while two hundred and fifty coins fell upon the riverbank. When the bag was empty, the monkey tossed the leather pouch and bounded away.

Gathering the remaining coins, Ganga Ram sat weeping on the bank. Just then, Birbal, who was traveling back to Agra with a small escort, stopped his horse and inquired about the tragedy.

Hearing the milkman's confession, Birbal smiled with profound irony:

'Do not weep, Ganga Ram. Nature has settled your accounts with perfect mathematics. The money you earned from honest buttermilk fell safely upon the earth for you to keep. The money you earned by watering down milk with river water has returned directly to the river! Divine justice has merely separated the milk from the water.'

Humbled and repentant, Ganga Ram vowed never to dilute his milk again.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "The Price of Buttermilk"?
options: Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
